{{short description|Short-time Fourier transform with variable resolution}}
In mathematics and [[signal processing]], the '''constant-Q transform''' and '''variable-Q transform''', simply known as '''CQT''' and '''VQT''', transforms a data series to the [[frequency domain]]. It is related to the [[Fourier transform]]<ref name="b91">[[Judy Brown (physicist)|Judith C. Brown]], [http://www.wellesley.edu/Physics/brown/pubs/cq1stPaper.pdf Calculation of a constant Q spectral transform], ''J. Acoust. Soc. Am.'', 89(1):425–434, 1991.</ref> and very closely related to the complex [[Morlet wavelet]] transform.<ref>[https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Continuous_Wavelet_Transform.html Continuous Wavelet Transform] "When the mother wavelet can be interpreted as a windowed sinusoid (such as the Morlet wavelet), the wavelet transform can be interpreted as a constant-Q Fourier transform. Before the theory of wavelets, constant-Q Fourier transforms (such as obtained from a classic third-octave filter bank) were not easy to invert, because the basis signals were not orthogonal."</ref> Its design is suited for musical representation.

[[File:CQT-piano-chord.png|thumb|'''Constant-Q transform''' applied to the [[waveform]] of a [[C major]] piano [[Chord (music)|chord]]. The x-axis is [[frequency]], mapped to standard [[Pitch (music)|musical pitches]], from low (left) to high (right). The y-axis is time, starting from pressing the piano chord at the bottom, and releasing the piano chord at the top, 8 seconds later.

Darker pixels correspond to higher values of the Constant-Q transform. The peaks correspond closely to the precise frequencies of the vibrating piano strings. Thus the peaks can be used to detect the notes played on the piano. The lowest 3 peaks are the [[fundamental frequencies]] of the C major chord (C, E, G). Each string also vibrates at multiples of the fundamental, known as [[overtones]], which correspond to the remaining smaller peaks to the right of the fundamental pitches. The overtones are smaller in intensity than the fundamental pitch.

[[File:Piano-C-major-chord.ogg|thumb|Audio of the C Major piano chord used to generate the Constant-Q transform above.]]

[[File:C-major-piano-chord-waveform.png|thumb|Its waveform does not visually communicate pitch information like the Constant-Q transform is able to do.]]]]

The transform can be thought of as a series of filters ''f''<sub>''k''</sub>, logarithmically spaced in frequency, with the ''k''-th filter having a [[spectral width]] ''δf''<sub>''k''</sub> equal to a multiple of the previous filter's width:

:<math>\delta f_k = 2^{1/n} \cdot \delta f_{k-1}
= \left( 2^{1/n} \right)^k \cdot \delta f_\text{min},</math>

where ''δf''<sub>''k''</sub> is the bandwidth of the ''k''-th filter, ''f''<sub>min</sub> is the central frequency of the lowest filter, and ''n'' is the number of filters per [[octave (electronics)|octave]].

== Calculation ==

The [[short-time Fourier transform]] of ''x''[''n''] for a frame shifted to sample ''m'' is calculated as follows:

:<math>X[k,m] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} W[n-m] x[n] e^{-j 2 \pi k n/N}. </math>

Given a data series at sampling frequency ''f''<sub>s</sub> = 1/''T'', ''T'' being the sampling period of our data, for each frequency bin we can define the following:
* Filter width, ''δf''<sub>''k''</sub>.
* ''Q'', the "quality factor":
:: <math> Q = \frac{f_k}{\delta f_k}.</math>
: This is shown below to be the integer number of cycles processed at a center frequency ''f<sub>k</sub>''.  As such, this somewhat defines the [[time complexity]] of the transform.
* Window length for the ''k''-th bin:
::<math> N[k] = \frac{f_\text{s}}{\delta f_k} = \frac{f_\text{s}}{f_k} Q. </math>
:Since ''f<sub>s</sub>''/''f<sub>k</sub>'' is the number of samples processed per cycle at frequency ''f<sub>k</sub>'', ''Q'' is the number of integer cycles processed at this central frequency.

The equivalent transform kernel can be found by using the following substitutions:
* The window length of each bin is now a function of the bin number:
::<math>N = N[k] = Q \frac{f_\text{s}}{f_k}.</math>
* The relative power of each bin will decrease at higher frequencies, as these sum over fewer terms.  To compensate for this, we normalize by ''N''[''k''].
* Any windowing function will be a function of window length, and likewise a function of window number.  For example, the equivalent [[Hamming window]] would be
::<math> W[k,n] = \alpha - (1 - \alpha) \cos \frac{2 \pi n}{N[k] - 1}, \quad  \alpha = 25/46, \quad 0 \leqslant n \leqslant N[k] - 1.</math>
* Our digital frequency, <math> \frac{2 \pi k}{N} </math>, becomes <math> \frac{2 \pi Q}{N[k]} </math>.

After these modifications, we are left with
:<math>X[k] = \frac{1}{N[k]} \sum_{n=0}^{N[k]-1} W[k,n] x[n] e^{\frac{-j2 \pi Qn}{N[k]}}. </math>

=== Variable-Q bandwidth calculation ===
{{More citations needed|section|find=variable q transform|date=August 2022}}
The variable-Q transform is the same as constant-Q transform, but the only difference is the filter Q is variable, hence the name variable-Q transform. The variable-Q transform is useful {{example needed span|plural=y|where time resolution on low frequencies is important|date=July 2023}}. There are ways to calculate the bandwidth of the VQT, one of them using [[equivalent rectangular bandwidth]] as a value for VQT bin's bandwidth.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Cwitkowitz|first1= Frank C.Jr|date= 2019|title= End-to-End Music Transcription Using Fine-Tuned Variable-Q Filterbanks|url= https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/232143614.pdf|journal= Rochester Institute of Technology|volume= |issue= |pages= 32–34|doi= |access-date=2022-08-21}}</ref>

The simplest way to implement a variable-Q transform is add a bandwidth offset called ''γ'' like this one:{{cn|date=August 2022}}

:<math> \delta f_k = \left(\frac{2}{f_k + \gamma} \right) Q. </math>

This formula can be modified to have extra parameters to adjust sharpness of the transition between constant-Q and constant-bandwidth like this:{{cn|date=January 2023}}

:<math> \delta f_k = \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt[\alpha]{f_k^\alpha + \gamma^\alpha}} \right) Q. </math>

with ''α'' as a parameter for transition sharpness and where ''α'' of 2 is equals to [[hyperbolic sine]] frequency scale, in terms of frequency resolution.

==Fast calculation==

The direct calculation of the constant-Q transform (either using naive [[discrete Fourier transform]] or slightly faster [[Goertzel algorithm]]) is slow when compared against the [[fast Fourier transform]]. However, the fast Fourier transform can itself be employed, in conjunction with the use of a [[Kernel (statistics)|kernel]], to perform the equivalent calculation but much faster.<ref name="pb92">[[Judy Brown (physicist)|Judith C. Brown]] and Miller S. Puckette, [http://academics.wellesley.edu/Physics/brown/pubs/effalgV92P2698-P2701.pdf An efficient algorithm for the calculation of a constant Q transform], ''J. Acoust. Soc. Am.'', 92(5):2698–2701, 1992.</ref> An approximate inverse to such an implementation was proposed in 2006; it works by going back to the discrete Fourier transform, and is only suitable for pitch instruments.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=FitzGerald |first1=Derry |last2=Cychowski |first2=Marcin T. |last3=Cranitch |first3=Matt |title=Towards an Inverse Constant Q Transform |journal=Audio Engineering Society Convention |date=1 May 2006 |volume=120 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228680714 |publisher=Audio Engineering Society |location=Paris |language=English}}</ref>

A development on this method with improved invertibility involves performing CQT (via fast Fourier transform) octave-by-octave, using lowpass filtered and downsampled results for consecutively lower pitches.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Schörkhuber |first1=Christian |last2=Klapuri |first2=Anssi |title=Constant-Q Transform Toolbox for Music Processing |conference=7th Sound and Music Computing Conference |date=2010 |url=https://www.iem.at/~schoerkhuber/cqt2010/ |accessdate=12 December 2018 |location=Barcelona }} [https://iem.kug.ac.at/fileadmin/media/iem/projects/2010/smc10_schoerkhuber.pdf paper] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201155825/https://iem.kug.ac.at/fileadmin/media/iem/projects/2010/smc10_schoerkhuber.pdf |date=2020-12-01 }}</ref> Implementations of this method include the [[MATLAB]] implementation and LibROSA's Python implementation.<ref name=librosa-cqt>{{cite web |last1=McFee |first1=Brian |last2=Battenberg |first2=Eric |last3=Lostanlen |first3=Vincent |last4=Thomé |first4=Carl |title=librosa: core/constantq.py at 8d26423 |url=https://github.com/librosa/librosa/blob/8d26423/librosa/core/constantq.py |website=GitHub |publisher=librosa |accessdate=12 December 2018 |date=12 December 2018}}</ref> LibROSA combines the subsampled method with the direct fast Fourier transform method (which it dubs "pseudo-CQT") by having the latter process higher frequencies as a whole.<ref name=librosa-cqt/>

The [[sliding discrete Fourier transform]] can be used for faster calculation of constant-Q transform, since the sliding discrete Fourier transform does not have to be linear-frequency spacing and same window size per bin.<ref name="cqsdft">Bradford, R, ffitch, J & Dobson, R 2008, [https://purehost.bath.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/377255/constQ.pdf Sliding with a constant-Q], in ''11th International Conference on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx-08) Proceedings September 1-4th, 2008 Espoo, Finland'' . DAFx, Espoo, Finland, pp. 363-369, Proc. of the Int. Conf. on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx-08), 1/09/08.</ref>

Alternatively, the constant-Q transform can be approximated by using multiple fast Fourier transforms of different window sizes and/or sampling rate at different frequency ranges then stitch it together. This is called multiresolution [[short-time Fourier transform]], however the window sizes for multiresolution fast Fourier transforms are different per-octave, rather than per-bin.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kırbız |first1=S. |last2=Günsel |first2=B. |date=December 2014 |title=A multiresolution non-negative tensor factorization approach for single channel sound source separation |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.sigpro.2014.05.019 |journal=Signal Processing |volume=105 |pages=56–69 |doi=10.1016/j.sigpro.2014.05.019 |bibcode=2014SigPr.105...56K |issn=0165-1684|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{ambiguous|reason=How multiresolution STFT are done?|date=December 2022}}
{{Expand section |1=nonstationary Gabor frames [https://www.univie.ac.at/nonstatgab/cqt/ as described here] (and [https://www.mathworks.com/help/wavelet/gs/non-stationary-gabor-frames.html as used by Matlab])|section=2 |date= December 2018}}

== Comparison with the Fourier transform ==

In general, the transform is well suited to musical data, and this can be seen in some of its advantages compared to the fast Fourier transform.  As the output of the transform is effectively amplitude/phase against log frequency, fewer frequency bins are required to cover a given range effectively, and this proves useful where frequencies span several octaves.  As the range of human hearing covers approximately ten octaves from 20&nbsp;Hz to around 20&nbsp;kHz, this reduction in output data is significant.

The transform exhibits a reduction in frequency resolution with higher frequency bins, which is desirable for auditory applications. The transform mirrors the human auditory system, whereby at lower-frequencies [[spectral resolution]] is better, whereas [[temporal resolution]] improves at higher frequencies. At the bottom of the piano scale (about 30&nbsp;Hz), a difference of 1 [[semitone]] is a difference of approximately 1.5&nbsp;Hz, whereas at the top of the musical scale (about 5&nbsp;kHz), a difference of 1 semitone is a difference of approximately 200&nbsp;Hz. So for musical data the exponential frequency resolution of constant-Q transform is ideal.

In addition, the harmonics of musical notes form a pattern characteristic of the timbre of the instrument in this transform.  Assuming the same relative strengths of each harmonic, as the fundamental frequency changes, the relative position of these harmonics remains constant.  This can make identification of instruments much easier. The constant Q transform can also be used for automatic recognition of musical keys based on accumulated chroma content.<ref name="pbo01">Hendrik Purwins, Benjamin Blankertz and Klaus Obermayer, [https://web.archive.org/web/20170109113106/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/f671/2e765320de050afd8305401b74a489d92c28.pdf A New Method for Tracking Modulations in Tonal Music in Audio Data Format], ''International Joint Conference on Neural Network (IJCNN’00).'', 6:270-275, 2000.</ref>

Relative to the Fourier transform, implementation of this transform is more tricky.  This is due to the varying number of samples used in the calculation of each frequency bin, which also affects the length of any windowing function implemented.<ref name="gb1999">Benjamin Blankertz, [https://doc.ml.tu-berlin.de/bbci/material/publications/Bla_constQ.pdf The Constant Q Transform], 1999.</ref>

Also note that because the frequency scale is logarithmic, there is no true zero-frequency / DC term present, which may be a drawback in applications that are interested in the DC term.  Although for applications that are not interested in the DC such as audio, this is not a drawback.
